distractorExplanations.a: PPE comes after elimination, substitution, engineering, and administrative controls, not before machine guarding.
distractorExplanations.c: PPE supplements engineering controls; it does not replace guards or ventilation that remove the hazard.
distractorExplanations.d: In the hierarchy, PPE ranks below administrative controls as the last line of defense.

options.text: Deduct the cost of required PPE from pay
Provide required PPE and training on use
Provide PPE but leave training to the vendor
Pay for everyday safety-toe boots worn off-site

explanation: Provide required PPE and training on use.

distractorExplanations.a: Under 1910.132(h), employers pay for required PPE, with limited exceptions such as everyday safety-toe footwear.
distractorExplanations.c: 1910.132(f) makes the employer responsible for training each worker on when and how to use PPE.
distractorExplanations.d: Non-specialty safety-toe footwear that workers may wear off the job is an exception to employer payment.

options.text: Impact and penetration hazards to the head
Noise exposures above the 85 dBA action level
Arc flash burns to the face and neck
Falls from heights above four feet

explanation: Impact and penetration hazards to the head.

distractorExplanations.b: Noise above the action level calls for hearing protection, not a hard hat.
distractorExplanations.c: Arc flash protection needs arc-rated face shields and clothing; a hard hat alone does not protect the face.
distractorExplanations.d: Falls are prevented by guardrails or fall arrest systems; hard hats protect against impact to the head.

options.text: Glasses with side shields seal better against splash
They give the same splash protection if rated Z87
Goggles are rated for impact but not for splash
Goggles generally seal better against splash

explanation: Goggles generally seal better against splash.

distractorExplanations.a: Side shields add impact protection from the side but do not seal; goggles are needed for splash.
distractorExplanations.b: The Z87 mark covers impact; splash protection requires goggles marked D3 for droplets and splash.
distractorExplanations.c: Reverses the point: goggles seal around the eyes and are the choice for chemical splash.

options.text: Noise exceeds 100 dBA for any length of time
A worker first reports ringing in the ears
Noise exceeds 90 dBA averaged over a full week
Noise exposures warrant it under the program

explanation: Noise exposures warrant it under the program.

distractorExplanations.a: The trigger is the 85 dBA 8-hour TWA action level; 100 dBA is just one point on the exposure table.
distractorExplanations.b: Ringing is a symptom of damage already done; protection is based on measured exposure, before symptoms.
distractorExplanations.c: OSHA noise limits use an 8-hour time-weighted average, not a weekly average.

options.text: The chemical or cut hazard
The worker's preferred grip feel
One general-purpose cotton type
The thickest material on hand

explanation: The chemical or cut hazard.

distractorExplanations.b: Comfort matters, but glove material must be chosen for the specific chemical or cut hazard first.
distractorExplanations.c: Cotton absorbs chemicals and offers little cut resistance; no single glove fits every hazard.
distractorExplanations.d: Thickness is not chemical resistance; permeation depends on glove material matched to the chemical.

options.text: Fit testing once at hire, with no medical evaluation required
A shared respirator cleaned at the end of each week
Medical clearance, training, and fit testing when applicable
Training only, since N95 masks need no fit test

explanation: Medical clearance, training, and fit testing when applicable.

distractorExplanations.a: 1910.134 requires a medical evaluation before use and fit testing annually, not once at hire.
distractorExplanations.b: Shared respirators must be cleaned and disinfected before being worn by another person, not weekly.
distractorExplanations.d: Required N95 filtering facepieces are tight-fitting and do need fit testing under the respiratory program.

options.text: Anchored to any fixed pipe or conduit nearby
Inspected once a year by the manufacturer
Kept in service after arresting a fall
Inspected and used correctly for the task

explanation: Inspected and used correctly for the task.

distractorExplanations.a: Anchors must support 5,000 lb per worker or be engineered; pipes and conduit are not rated anchorages.
distractorExplanations.b: Users inspect fall protection before each use, with periodic competent-person checks, not a yearly factory check.
distractorExplanations.c: Equipment that has arrested a fall must be removed from service until a competent person clears it.

options.text: Replace barriers and flaggers between workers and traffic
Workers be seen by vehicle and equipment operators
Protect workers from cuts and abrasions
Workers stay cool under direct sunlight

explanation: Workers be seen by vehicle and equipment operators.

distractorExplanations.a: High-visibility apparel adds conspicuity; it does not replace physical barriers or flaggers in work zones.
distractorExplanations.c: Hi-vis garments are about being seen; cut protection comes from gloves and cut-resistant sleeves.
distractorExplanations.d: Hi-vis colors are chosen for visibility, not cooling; heat stress needs water, rest, and shade.

options.text: Repaired with duct tape
Removed from service
Used until the shift ends
Cleaned and reissued

explanation: Removed from service.

distractorExplanations.a: Improvised repairs do not restore the rated protection; damaged PPE must be taken out of service.
distractorExplanations.c: Damaged PPE may fail during the shift; it must be removed from service as soon as damage is found.
distractorExplanations.d: Cleaning does not fix cracks, tears, or worn parts; damaged PPE is removed from service, not reissued.

options.text: Slips on wet or oily floors
Ankle sprains on uneven ground
Compression and impact to toes
Chemical splashes on the shin

distractorExplanations.a: Slip resistance comes from the outsole tread and compound, not from the steel toe cap.
distractorExplanations.b: Ankle support depends on boot height and fit; a steel toe protects the toes, not the ankle.
distractorExplanations.d: Shin splash protection needs chemical-resistant boots or covers; the steel toe protects against impact and compression.

options.text: Hard hats for overhead impact
Safety glasses for impact/splash
Respirators for vapor exposure
Hearing protection for noise

explanation: Safety glasses for impact/splash — they may not replace primary eye protection alone. Face shields are secondary protection worn over safety glasses or goggles; they may not replace primary eye protection alone.

distractorExplanations.a: Face shields protect the face, not the head; overhead impact protection comes from the hard hat.
distractorExplanations.c: A face shield does not filter air; vapor exposure is handled by ventilation or respirators.
distractorExplanations.d: A face shield does nothing for noise; hearing protection is a separate piece of PPE.

options.text: Workers handle flammable liquids
Voltage is below 50 volts
Work is done on de-energized gear
Electrical arc hazards exist

explanation: Electrical arc hazards exist.

distractorExplanations.a: Flammable liquid handling calls for ignition control and flame-resistant clothing for flash fire, not arc-rated gear.
distractorExplanations.b: Below 50 volts, NFPA 70E generally does not require arc flash protection; arc-rated gear applies where arc hazards exist.
distractorExplanations.c: Equipment verified de-energized under lockout/tagout has no arc hazard, so arc-rated clothing is not the trigger.
